charts.title: Same sepsis spec, three engines: where compute time goes (committed full-run + live per-step)
charts.caption: Two views of where the compute goes for the same sepsis spec. Left: full 48 h run wall-clock under BioGears (~3.38 h), Tellurium exact SBML (~2.81 h), and the PyTorch surrogate (~0.2 s) — committed numbers. Right: live per-step cost measured on this machine — one exact CVODE step of the real 91-state model ~526 ms vs one surrogate forward pass ~0.04 ms (exact is ~13,000x; exact values from bench_live.json). Both show the same thing: the exact engines spend their time in the stiff ODE solve; the surrogate replaces it with a forward pass.
charts.interpretation: Wall-clock for one matched 48 h severe-sepsis run of the SAME model specification, executed by three interchangeable engines. BioGears 8.2.0 (the original C++ whole-body physiology engine) takes ~3.38 h; the Tellurium/roadrunner exact-SBML extraction of the same core takes ~2.81 h (BioGears + Tellurium figures are committed meta.wall_s from the engine-runtime data consolidated into this study). Both are dominated by the same cost: integrating the stiff 91-state ODE (a stiff implicit solver, CVODE, is required and already compiled C). A PyTorch neural surrogate of the same core runs the 48 h / 576-step rollout in ~0.2 s — roughly 40,000x faster than the exact SBML path — because it replaces the ODE solve with one forward pass per step. The surrogate trades accuracy for speed (it stays bounded over the horizon but is NOT clinically accurate — in fact degenerate across severity; see study 05), so it is a fast approximate tier, not a drop-in replacement. The point of the figure is the span: the same spec runs across four-plus orders of magnitude of compute by swapping the engine, and the compute in the exact engines is spent almost entirely in stiff ODE integration.
charts.key: Same sepsis spec, three engines: where compute time goes (committed full-run + live per-step)

charts.title: Surrogate admissibility on severe sepsis — 8 of 9 observables leave physical bounds
charts.caption: Surrogate predictions on the severe arm (severity 3, 48 h, at the surrogate's trained 300 s timestep) checked against physical bounds. 8 of 9 observables leave admissible ranges: SBP, DBP, MAP, HR, CO, blood_volume, tissue_integrity, blood_pathogen — the surrogate reaches MAP ≈ -158 mmHg, tissue integrity ≈ -6.1, and negative blood pathogen, all physically impossible. So on severe sepsis the surrogate is not admissible, let alone mechanistically accurate: speed does not help here, and the exact engine is required. A fair held-out-severity admissibility protocol at the trained timestep is the pending validator (study 07, SURR-01).
charts.key: Surrogate admissibility on severe sepsis — 8 of 9 observables leave physical bounds

charts.title: Same sepsis SBML, two exact engines — Tellurium and COPASI agree to ~5e-4, at 4.7× the cost
charts.caption: The identical BioGears-sepsis SBML (severe, 2 h) under the main engine Tellurium (roadrunner/CVODE) and a second independent exact-SBML integrator, COPASI (LSODA, driven through libCOPASI directly). The two agree to within 5.0e-04 across all nine shared observables — the exact-SBML result is engine-independent, not a roadrunner artifact. The agreement costs 4.7× more wall-clock in COPASI (168 s vs 784 s): the model is event-dense (the per-beat event), and COPASI evaluates each event through an interpreted math layer while roadrunner runs LLVM-compiled code.
charts.key: Same sepsis SBML, two exact engines — Tellurium and COPASI agree to ~5e-4, at 4.7× the cost
